ObjectName.value: Bear Shooters, 1930

Categories.value: Bear Shooters|Media from YouTube|WebM videos|PD US not renewed|Files uploaded by Yann Forget|Uploaded with video2commons|Video display resolution 480 x 360

ImageDescription.value:
Bear Shooters is a 1930 Our Gang short comedy film directed by Robert F. McGowan. It was the 98th (tenth talking) Our Gang short that was released.

Plot:

Spud wants to go camping and shoot lots of bears with Jackie, Chubby, and Farina. But his mother has forced him to look after his little brother Wheezer, who has the croup. In caring for his brother he must periodically apply ointment to his chest. He tells his friends he must stay home and grease Wheezer. He tries to get his sister Mary Ann to do this but she insists on going camping. Spud decides to merely go camping anyway and take both Wheezer and Mary Ann along. The gang all go together in an old dilapidated wagon guided by Dinah The Mule. The trip initially goes smoothly, but after some time two bootleggers who have themselves concealed in the area spot the gang and decide to try to get the gang to leave. One of the bootleggers dresses up like an ape in order to scare the gang away. While he scares the gang, the gang manages to trap the ape. Eventually the gang ends up leaving the forest due to a skunk spraying the area, not the bootlegger in the ape suit.

ObjectName.value: Brown bear itching back on tree - Deshaker

Categories.value: Self-published work|Videos from South Dakota|Bear Country USA|Ursus arctos in zoos|Ursidae in zoos in the United States|Animals scratching against trees|Videos of Ursus arctos|Videos at zoos in the United States|Videos of animal behavior

ImageDescription.value:
A brown bear scratching his/her back on a downed tree in Bear Country USA, which is right outside of Rapid City, South Dakota.

This is a derivative work of Joe Chill 2's File:Brown bear itching back on tree.ogv (2010-06-19). I removed as much camera shaking as I could, using Gunnar Thalin's Deshaker plugin for VirtualDub. I also removed as much of the rolling-shutter artifacts as I could, but couldn't remove them completely, due to not knowing what camera was used, the large macroblocks of the high compression originally used, and possibly also limitations of Deshaker.

Since the framerate is NTSC's 29.97, I looked at changing the pixel aspect ratio to be 4:3 rather than the 720x480 video's claimed 1:1, but I couldn't tell for sure whether that was correct, so left it as-is. Some jerkiness remains due to lots of missing frames in the video (yet the original .ogv metadata claimed it was fixed rather than variable framerate). That plus the lack of zooming and the high compression would seem to indicate this was shot on a 2010-era cellphone, which would make the original pixel aspect ratio more likely to be 1:1 than 4:3.

I was originally going to upload this as a new revision of the original .ogv file, but per Help:Converting video's recommendations, I encoded to VP9/webm, and you can't change video formats in a new revision, nor can you rename the file in one.

Credit.value: Own work

ImageDescription.value:
A grizzly bear at the Grizzly & Wolf Discovery Center plays, and films himself with, a GoPro.
Original description:
Two videos taken by grizzly bears at the Grizzy & Wolf Discovery Center, West Yellowstone, Montana. The bears found a previously-lost GoPro Hero 11 in a protective case, in their pond, which had enough battery left to take a couple of brief shots, including a selfie.
As these video files were created entirely by bears, by accident, I believe them to be in the public domain. If that's not the case, then as the owner of the camera and potential copyright holder, I'm happy to license these files under CC0 and dedicate them to the public domain as far as legally possible.
If you do use these files, it'd be nice to make a donation to the Grizzly & Wolf Discovery Center. They've got bears to feed.
